name: AI Champions in Every Building
title: AI Champions in Every Building
answer: An AI champion is a teacher in each school building who uses AI thoughtfully and helps colleagues do the same, so that support sits where teachers actually work. It matters because change spreads through people teachers trust, and a champion turns shared leadership into everyday help rather than a distant policy. The role only works when the school gives the champion time and support, and when the champion is honest about AI's limits rather than enthusiastic about everything.

sections.body: This idea places one teacher in every building as an AI champion, someone who uses AI carefully and can answer colleagues' questions close to their classrooms. It solves a practical problem: support and guidance are often far away from where teachers work, so interest fades before it becomes practice. The champion is a form of shared leadership, which research on principals spreading AI policy found was central to their approach. The role is not about being the most excited person in the building. The goal is good judgment, and a champion who acknowledges what AI cannot do often carries more credibility with skeptical colleagues than one who praises everything.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, the champion is a colleague teachers already trust, available in the building to show how AI is used thoughtfully and to talk through questions as they come up. Because the role sits on top of a full teaching load, the district should provide release time, a small stipend, or reduced duties so the champion does not burn out. Champions should also meet across buildings to share what they learn, so one school's experience reaches the others. The text does not give grade band examples, so the arrangement applies to any building where a teacher takes on the role. Schools should also choose champions who represent a range of views, since a thoughtful champion who is honest about AI's limits often helps skeptical colleagues more than an enthusiastic one.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels this idea with research, citing a study on principals spreading AI policy which found that shared leadership was central to their approach (Avidov-Ungar & Ganon-Shilon, 2026). The book uses that finding to support champions as a form of shared leadership. No other study, figure or finding is given for the champion role itself, so the practical claims about time, stipends and credibility rest on the book's own guidance rather than additional research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main limit is time: a champion expected to help colleagues on top of a full teaching load will burn out, so districts should provide release time, a small stipend, or reduced duties. A second risk is credibility, because a champion who is enthusiastic about everything may not help skeptical colleagues, while one who is honest about AI's limits often has more credibility. The text also warns against the role becoming cheerleading, since the goal is good judgment. The decisions about who champions are, what support they receive, and how they represent a range of views stay with the district and school leaders, not with the AI itself.
